title: How would you keep an AI narrator from deciding what a player feels about their backstory?
author: yrovex
selftext:
I’m building SOUL RP, a free Bleach-inspired text RPG. One scene in Void starts with a fact the character can’t change: a captain saved their class years ago. That fact belongs in the character’s history. I don’t want the model to infer that the player trusts the captain just because the rescue is in context.



The test I’d run has three versions of the same tribunal scene. The player says they’re grateful, says they resent the captain, or says nothing about it at all. The narrator should remember the same rescue in each run. Classmates can have their own opinions, but in the silent run the model shouldn’t put gratitude or resentment in the player’s mouth.



For those building character memory: would you store explicit player stances separately from shared events, or leave the stance unset and ask for it in dialogue? What would you test to catch the model treating an NPC’s opinion as the player’s?

comments.author: No-Pollution7797
comments.body:
I'd store them separately, and I'd treat unset as a real value rather than a blank. A blank tends to get filled, since a rescue sitting in context with no stance next to it reads to the model like an invitation to supply the obvious one, so I'd have the record say outright that the player hasn't said how they feel about it yet. Then the narrator's job in the silent run is to describe what the character does and what others assume, and leave the inside of their head alone.



For the test, I'd check the silent run for any sentence where the player character is the subject of a feeling verb about the captain (trusts, owes, resents), and separately run a version where a classmate states a strong opinion right before the player's turn. That second one is where the bleed usually shows up, the narrator quietly adopts whatever the last NPC said as the mood of the scene.
